newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest Nov hydropower down slightly on yr.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest Nov hydropower down slightly on yr.

text.p: Power output at U.S. Northwest hydroelectric power dams operated by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers fell slightly in November compared with the same 1995 month, a spokesman for the Corps said Monday.
Net generation in November totaled 4.036 million megawatt hours (MWh), compared with 4.823 million in November 1995.
Projects operated by the Corps of Engineers account for about 50 percent of total regional hydropower generation. The power is marketed by Bonneville Power Administration.
The Corps spokesman noted colder temperatures a year ago contributed to the higher 1995 output because there was more load to supply power to.
"You can only generate power when you have someone on the other end to turn on the lights," he explained.
Systemwide capacity on the Corps projects is about 13,000 average megawatts, compared with a normal peak of just 8,000 or so.
The spokesman said there were very few operational constraints on the hydropower system at this stage of the season this year, with projections calling for ample water supplies through next spring.
"Rain doesn't really affect our power generation - most projects are on the Columbia (River) which is mostly snow-fed," he noted.
The Corps' net hydropower generation during October, the first month of the current water year, was 3.977 million MWh, up from 3.911 million in the same 1995 month.
According to the National Weather Service, precipitation for the Columbia River basin was 129 percent of normal average levels in November, compared with 174 percent of normal a year earlier.
